articles.title: Acute relationships between changes in iliotibial band shear wave velocity and lower-limb muscle activity during a single-leg press exercise.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to explore the associations between acute changes in iliotibial band (ITB) shear wave velocity (SWV) and changes in the SWV of anatomically related muscles, as well as the association between muscle activity during a seated single-leg press exercise and post-exercise ITB SWV. METHODS: Twenty healthy adults performed five sets of 20 single-leg press repetitions at 50 % of their estimated maximal lower-limb extension strength. SWV was measured before and after the experimental protocol in the ITB, tensor fasciae latae (TFL), gluteus maximus (Gmax), gluteus medius (Gmed), and vastus lateralis (VL). Muscle activity during the fifth set was assessed using surface electromyography and normalized to maximal voluntary contraction. Associations were examined using Spearman's rank correlation coefficients with bias-corrected and accelerated 95 % confidence intervals. RESULTS: VL SWV significantly decreased following the experimental protocol (Holm-adjusted p < 0.005), whereas no significant pre-post changes were observed in the ITB, TFL, Gmax, or Gmed. No significant correlations were found between the percentage change in ITB SWV and the percentage changes in adjacent-muscle SWV (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.768). Post-exercise ITB SWV was not significantly correlated with muscle activity of any examined muscle (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.596). CONCLUSION: Under the experimental conditions, changes in ITB SWV were not significantly associated with concurrent changes in adjacent-muscle SWV, and post-exercise ITB SWV was not significantly associated with muscle activity during the exercise.

articles.title: Using a sacral cluster to improve pelvic tracking during gait in overweight individuals.
articles.authors: N B J Dur, L M S Damink, E M Macri et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pelvic tracking in three-dimensional (3D) human motion analysis commonly uses skin-mounted anterior superior iliac spines (ASIS) markers. However, these conventional methods are prone to soft tissue artifacts, especially in overweight individuals. Using a sacral marker cluster with pointer-defined virtual ASIS markers might be an alternative approach for more accurate pelvic tracking across different body compositions. RESEARCH QUESTION: What are the differences in pelvic and hip joint mechanics measured during gait using conventional pelvic tracking versus pelvic tracking with a sacral cluster in healthy-weight and overweight individuals? METHODS: Ten healthy-weight and ten overweight/obese participants underwent 3D gait analysis. The pelvis was simultaneously tracked using skin-mounted markers and a sacral cluster with pointer-defined virtual ASIS markers. Pelvic kinematics and hip kinematics and kinetics were compared between tracking methods using statistical parametric mapping paired t-tests. Root mean squared differences (RMSD) and paired Cohen's dz were calculated for significantly different waveform regions. RESULTS: Frontal-plane pelvic kinematics differed between methods more substantially in the overweight group (RMSD=4.6° ± 1.7°, dz=-0.9) than in the healthy-weight group (RMSD=2.8° ± 0.8°, dz=0.3). Frontal-plane hip kinematics also differed more substantially in the overweight group (RMSD=5.4° ± 2.3°, dz=-0.8) than in the healthy-weight group (RMSD=2.7° ± 1.7°, dz=1.4). Hip kinetics differed mostly in the sagittal plane, with more substantial differences in the overweight group (RMSD=0.22 ± 0.09Nm/kg, dz=2.3) than in the healthy-weight group (RMSD=0.11 ± 0.04Nm/kg, dz=2.7). DISCUSSION: Pelvic tracking using a sacral cluster with pointer-defined virtual ASIS markers provides different, and potentially more accurate, pelvic and hip mechanics across different body compositions than conventional methods using skin-mounted ASIS markers.

articles.title: Effect Of Joint-Angle Configuration on Hamstring Torque-Duration Relationship Parameters and the Etiology of Motor Performance Fatigue.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Baptiste Corcelle, Gregory M Blain, Pierre Demeusoy et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study examined how hamstring muscle-tendon unit length influences critical torque (CT), work capacity above CT (W'), and the mechanisms of motor performance fatigue during and after repeated maximal voluntary contractions. METHODS: Twelve healthy men (25 ± 4 years) performed, on separate days, two fatiguing protocols consisting of fifty 3-s maximal isometric knee flexions (2-s rest) at joint-angle configurations expected to produce relatively long (LL) and short (SL) hamstring muscle-tendon unit lengths. Neuromuscular assessments were conducted before, during, and up to 15 min post-exercise. CT and W' were determined from the torque-duration relationship. Peripheral fatigue was evaluated using peak evoked torques (T100), and central fatigue using voluntary activation (VA) derived from the twitch interpolation technique. Linear mixed-effects models and paired t-tests assessed the effects of time and joint-angle configuration. RESULTS: CT did not differ between LL and SL (p = 0.65), whereas W' was significantly lower at SL than LL (p < 0.001, d = 0.96). MVC torque decreased by ~45% after fatiguing protocols (p < 0.001, η 2p = 0.84), accompanied by reductions in T100 (-22%) and VA (-17). During recovery, VA returned to baseline within 3 min, while T100 remained depressed throughout recovery (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In the knee flexors, short muscle-tendon unit length reduces the capacity to perform work above CT without altering CT or the magnitude and etiology of fatigue. The rapid recovery of voluntary activation alongside persistent peripheral impairment extends current knowledge of recovery kinetics specifically for repeated maximal knee-flexion exercise.

articles.title: Low-Intensity Resistance Training Improves Irisin-Associated Endothelial Function in Aging.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Sosuke Yasunaga, Shumpei Fujie, Reita Ito et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Low-intensity resistance training (LRT) may be suitable for both muscle and cardiovascular health of older adults. However, its effects and mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to examine whether LRT improves endothelial function in adult senescence-accelerated mouse prone 1 (SAMP1) mice, a model of accelerated aging, and whether this response is accompanied by changes in circulating irisin, arterial protein kinase B (Akt)/endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) signaling, and nitric oxide (NO) levels. METHODS: Adult (38-week-old) SAMP1 mice were randomized to three groups: LRT (climbing a ladder at 40% maximal carrying capacity, 3 days/week for 12 weeks), high-intensity resistance training (80%), or sedentary control, with assessment at 50 weeks of age. Young (13-week-old) SAMP1 mice were used as a sedentary-control group. In the human study, 17 healthy middle-aged and older adults were allocated to an LRT or control group in a randomized controlled trial. LRT participants performed an elastic band-based resistance training program for 45 min, three times per week, for 8 weeks. RESULTS: In adult mice, aging was associated with reduced circulating irisin levels and muscle fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5 (FNDC5) expression, accompanied by impaired endothelial function, diminished arterial NO production, and attenuated Akt/eNOS signaling. These age-related impairments were improved by LRT. Consistent with these findings in mice, LRT in middle-aged and older adults increased circulating nitrate/nitrite (NOx) and irisin concentrations, accompanied by improvements in endothelial function. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that LRT-induced enhancement of circulating irisin secretion in adult SAMP1 mice and middle-aged and older adults may be involved in the improvement of endothelial function accompanied by increased NO production and the activation of the arterial Akt/eNOS signaling pathway.

articles.title: Midlife Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Site-Specific Cancer Outcomes in Men.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Clare Meernik, David Leonard, Kerem Shuval et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Higher cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is associated with a lower risk of cancer and mortality after diagnosis. However, mortality data are generally not specific to cancer sites or causes of death, limiting insights into the underlying mechanisms and opportunities for targeted prevention and survivorship strategies. This study aimed to examine the association between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and mortality after diagnosis in men. METHODS: This cohort study used data from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (1971-2018) linked to Medicare claims (1999-2019). CRF was estimated using a maximal treadmill test. The associations between CRF and site-specific cancer incidence and death after cancer for the leading cancer sites in men (colorectal, lung, and prostate) were estimated using multivariable illness-death models and proportional hazards regression with Gompertz baseline hazards. RESULTS: Among 28,612 men with a mean Medicare follow-up of 7.9 years to cancer incidence, 4,998 colorectal, lung, and prostate cancers were identified. Higher CRF was associated with a lower risk of colorectal (HR: 0.91 per metabolic equivalent of task [MET]; 95% CI: 0.87, 0.96) and lung cancer (HR: 0.81 per MET; 95% CI: 0.77, 0.85), but not prostate cancer. During a mean follow-up of 7.1 years to death after diagnosis of colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer, 1,549 deaths were identified. High- (vs. low-) fit men with colorectal, lung, or prostate cancer had a 33-41% lower likelihood of all-cause mortality, including a generally lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease and other non-cancer causes. CONCLUSIONS: Achieving higher CRF levels may contribute to cancer prevention and longer survival after diagnosis. Interventions that increase CRF through physical activity may improve health across the cancer control continuum.

articles.title: Understanding the conceptual layers of 'sympathetic': Implications for autonomic neuroscience.
Three separate pancreatic acinar cell receptors employ different combinations of intracellular pathways to Ca2+ signalling.
articles.authors: Muhanad Salih, Julia V Gerasimenko, Oleg V Gerasimenko et al.
articles.abstract: Cytosolic Ca2+ spiking in pancreatic acinar cells, elicited by low concentrations of ACh, cholecystokinin (CCK) and gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), controls the secretion of digestive enzymes, whereas high-intensity stimulation induces sustained Ca2+ elevation initiating acute pancreatitis. Since the discovery of the Ca2+-releasing function of inositol 1,4,5-trisphophate (IP3), it has been assumed that Ca2+ signalling relies on the phospholipase C-IP3 pathway. We have now compared the mechanisms of action of the three physiological stimulants acting on three different receptors. Each pathway to Ca2+ signalling depends on functional IP3 receptors. However, low physiological concentrations of CCK and GRP, unlike ACh, cannot elicit Ca2+ signals without co-operation of an additional intracellular mechanism. CCK-elicited Ca2+ signalling has an absolute requirement for functional intracellular receptors for nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) but, surprisingly, does not depend on the activity of CD38, the enzyme involved in the synthesis of both NAADP and cyclic ADP ribose (cADPR). Thus, physiological CCK-evoked Ca2+ signalling requires functional NAADP and IP3 receptors, but not necessarily an increase in the production of these messengers. In contrast, GRP-elicited Ca2+ signal generation does not require functional NAADP receptors but does depend on the operation of CD38, indicating a requirement for increased cADPR production. Even Ca2+ signals elicited by ACh are partially dependent on CD38 but not on functional NAADP receptors. It is the engagement of non-IP3 pathways that allows low concentrations of secretagogues to elicit safe Ca2+ spiking and therefore secretion, obviating the need for potentially toxic high levels of agonists. KEY POINTS: Three different agonists acting on three different receptors, on the same normal pancreatic acinar cell, employ different combinations of intracellular pathways to generate cytosolic Ca2+ signals. Activation of IP3 receptors is always required for Ca2+ signal generation but is insufficient alone. At least two separate intracellular pathways and intracellular receptors are required for physiological Ca2+ signalling. Although functional IP3 receptors are always required, the second parallel pathway, and its relative importance, differs for the different agonists. The exceptionally high sensitivity of pancreatic acinar cells to physiological, low pico-molar, cholecystokinin (CCK) concentrations appears to be due to sensitization of IP3 and nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) receptors to resting messenger levels.

articles.title: Load Range During Isokinetic Knee Extension and Flexion Exercise in Strength-Matched Male and Female Collegiate Athletes.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Tianyi Lu, Marvin Powell, B Christine Green et al.
articles.abstract: Lu, T, Powell, M, Green, BC, Brown, LE, and Jones, MT. Load range during isokinetic knee extension and flexion exercise in strength-matched men and women collegiate athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Isokinetic testing is a quantitative and objective measure of muscular strength. Despite its accurate nature, mistakes may occur in interpretation of test results when not accounting for load range. The aim of this study was to quantify acceleration, deceleration, and load range across a velocity spectrum during concentric knee extension and flexion exercises on an isokinetic dynamometer and to investigate sex differences in these components among strength-matched male and female collegiate athletes. Thirty male (n = 15) and female (n = 15) collegiate track and field athletes performed maximal knee extension and flexion exercise at constant angular velocities of 60, 120, 180, 300, 350, and 400 deg·s-1. Load range is defined as the range during which the athlete's legs moved over 90% of the preset velocity. Repeated measures analysis of variance was applied to evaluate differences in acceleration, deceleration, and load range across angular velocities and sex. There was a significant main effect of angular velocity on all ranges in both knee extension and flexion (p < 0.001). Men exhibited smaller acceleration range at all conditions except for the knee extension at 120 deg·s-1 (p = 0.228, d = 0.28) and a larger load range at all conditions except for the knee extension at 120 deg·s-1 (p = 0.065, d = 0.57). Results suggest that despite being matched in relative strength, male athletes required less time to accelerate the limb to a desired velocity. Practitioners are recommended to use different protocols for male and female athletes when performing isokinetic training and testing.

articles.title: How Often Should Volume Increase? Effects of Different Volume-Progression Frequencies on Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Women.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Alysson Enes, Ana Carolina G Macedo, Guilherme Nass et al.
articles.abstract: Enes, A, Macedo, ACG, Nass, G, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Alves-Marques, F, Santana, C, Dell'Avanzi, FG, Rodrigues, BG, Alves, RC, De Souza, EO, and Souza-Junior, TP. How often should volume increase? Effects of different volume-progression frequencies on strength and hypertrophy adaptations in females. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Resistance training (RT) volume is an important programming variable for strength and hypertrophy. However, how frequently RT volume should be progressed remains unclear. Thus, we investigated the effects of progressively increasing RT volume by 2 weekly sets targeting the quadriceps femoris every 2 weeks (2 W) or every 4 weeks (4 W) over a 12-week period in recreationally trained women. Using a within-subject design and accounting for previous RT volume, 21 subjects (age 23.3 ± 3.9 years; RT experience 1.1 ± 0.7 years) had their limbs assigned to one of the 2 conditions: 2 weeks (2 W) or 4 weeks (4 W). 45° leg-press 1-repetition maximum (1RM) and the sum of muscle thickness (∑MT) of the proximal (30%), middle (50%), and distal (70%) portions of the lateral thigh were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect of time for 1RM (p < 0.0001), with no difference between the 2 and 4 W conditions (p = 0.317). Similarly, regarding the ∑MT, the analysis indicated a main effect of time (p < 0.001), with no difference between the conditions (p = 0.616). Within the relatively high training volumes examined, progressing the RT volume by 2 weekly sets every 2 or 4 weeks did not elicit detectable differences in strength and hypertrophy adaptations over 12 weeks in recreationally trained women.

articles.title: Dumbbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Fly Elicit Similar Pectoralis Major Muscle Hypertrophy in Recreationally Trained Men.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Filipi G Dell'Avanzi, Alysson Enes, Felipe Alves-Marques et al.
articles.abstract: Dell'Avanzi, FG, Enes, A, Alves-Marques, F, Costa-Rodrigues, J, Bello, G, Seima, G, Nass, G, Moreira, NF, Santana, C, Mohan, AE, Piñero, A, Schoenfeld, BJ, and Souza-Junior, TP. Dumbbell bench press and dumbbell fly elicit similar pectoralis major muscle hypertrophy in recreationally trained men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Exercise selection is one of the main resistance training (RT) variables for eliciting inhomogeneous muscle growth. Whether exercises that differ in resistance moment arm elicit whole- and nonuniform hypertrophy of the pectoralis major remains unclear. This study investigated the effects of the dumbbell bench press (DBP) and dumbbell fly (DFLY) on pectoralis major muscle thickness (MT). Twenty-six young healthy men (RT experience 3.3 ± 3.1 years) were allocated to DBP or DFLY groups, training twice a week over a 10-week period. The weekly set number was individualized according to subjects' previous RT pectoralis major volume. Pectoralis major MT was assessed by ultrasound imaging at medial (30%), intermediate (50%), and lateral (70%) sites at baseline and postintervention. Our mixed-model analysis indicated a main effect for time (p < 0.05) but no time-by-group interaction for the medial site (p = 0.500), intermediate site (p = 0.864), lateral site (p = 0.720), and the sum of the MT across sites (p = 0.985). Therefore, both exercises elicited similar general and regional hypertrophy on pectoralis major MT in recreationally trained individuals. Coaches and practitioners can select DBP or DFLY when targeting pectoralis major muscle development in recreationally trained men based on personal preference and goals within the RT program.

articles.title: Effect of Different Plyometric Training Protocols on Physical Fitness in Trained Youth Soccer Players.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Raouf Hammami, Abdelkader Mahmoudi, Wajdi Dardouri et al.
articles.abstract: Hammami, R, Mahmoudi, A, Dardouri, W, and van den Tillaar, R. Effect of different plyometric training protocols on physical fitness in trained youth soccer players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the effects of bilateral and unilateral plyometric training, performed at different volumes, on physical performance in trained youth male soccer players. Thirty-two subjects were randomly assigned to one of three 8-week plyometric training groups: bilateral (4 × 8 reps), high-volume unilateral (4 × 8 reps per leg), and low-volume unilateral (4 × 4 reps per leg). All groups completed 2 supervised sessions per week, with intensity increases adjusted according to individual readiness. Pre- and postintervention assessments included dynamic balance, maximal lower-limb strength (bilateral and unilateral 1 repetition maximum half squat), lower-limb power (five-jump test), linear sprint speed (10 and 30 m), and change-of-direction (CoD) ability. Significant improvements were observed over time for all performance measures (p ≤ 0.001, η2 ≥ 0.41). Unilateral plyometric training was associated with greater improvements in both bilateral and unilateral strength, and five-jump performance, compared with the bilateral condition, whereas CoD, sprint, and balance performance improved similarly across all groups, with no significant differences between training modalities. In addition, no differences were observed between the low- and high-volume unilateral protocols for any measured variables, suggesting that training volume within the tested range did not differentially affect outcomes. The findings indicate that incorporating plyometric training alongside regular soccer practice is associated with improvements in multiple aspects of physical performance in youth players. Within this context, unilateral plyometric training was associated with greater improvements in strength and power outcomes compared with bilateral training, whereas changes in sprint, CoD, and balance performance were similar across training modalities, suggesting that these capacities were not differentially influenced.

articles.title: Survival and functional outcomes in surgically treated pelvic chondrosarcoma: a retrospective single-center cohort study.
articles.authors: Niklas Deventer, Jan Christoph Theil, Georg Gosheger et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pelvic chondrosarcoma is a rare malignant bone tumor associated with challenging surgical management, high morbidity, and variable oncological outcomes. Because of its rarity, prognostic factors and functional outcomes remain insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated survival, prognostic factors, complications, and functional outcomes following surgical treatment of primary and locally recurrent pelvic chondrosarcoma. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 54 consecutive patients who underwent surgery for primary pelvic chondrosarcoma (n = 37) or locally recurrent disease (n = 17) at a single tertiary musculoskeletal oncology center between 2007 and 2020. Patients undergoing surgery for metastatic pelvic lesions were excluded. Overall survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Univariable Cox regression analyses and an exploratory multivariable model including age and tumor grade were performed. Functional outcome was assessed using the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society (MSTS) score. RESULTS: The mean clinical follow-up was 31.7 months. During follow-up, 22 patients died. Estimated overall survival was 80.3% at 1 year (95% CI 65.4-89.3%), 65.1% at 3 years (95% CI 48.6-77.4%), and 48.8% at 5 years (95% CI 30.6-64.8%). Increasing age was independently associated with a higher hazard of death (adjusted HR per year, 1.048; 95% CI, 1.014-1.083; p = 0.0052); tumor grade also showed an association (adjusted HR per grade, 1.802; 95% CI, 1.006-3.228; p = 0.0476). Functional outcome was available for 27 patients, with a mean MSTS score of 11.6 ± 5.8. Revision surgery was required in 38 patients (70.4%). CONCLUSIONS: Surgical treatment of pelvic chondrosarcoma is associated with considerable morbidity and impaired functional outcome. In this cohort, age and tumor grade were associated with overall survival in an exploratory model. These findings should be interpreted in light of the retrospective design, limited cohort size, and relatively short follow-up. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: not applicable.

articles.title: Aqua Steps: A Feasibility Study of a new Aquatic Exercise Therapy Intervention for Falls Prevention in Older Adults.
articles.authors: Stelios G Psycharakis, Linda Linton, John Norrie et al.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: One-third of people ≥65 years old fall at least once each year. Falls cause major deteriorations in physical and mental health and have high economic costs. Aquatic exercise may reduce falls, but research on older adults at high falls risk is sparse. OBJECTIVE: The objective was to assess the feasibility and acceptability of a new aquatic exercise intervention (Aqua Steps) and explore preliminary evidence on its effectiveness for older adults at high falls risk. DESIGN: A feasibility study for the Aqua Steps intervention, with secondary outcome assessments at baseline, end of intervention, and 6 months after end of intervention. A second group undertook an established pre-existing land-based program for falls prevention (Steady Steps). SETTING: The settings were swimming pools and exercise halls. PARTICIPANTS: Participants were 101 older adults at high falls risk. INTERVENTIONS: Both the aquatic and land-based group participants undertook 60 minutes of supervised exercise therapy per week, for 16 weeks. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcomes, based on Aqua Steps feasibility, included recruitment, retention, and adverse events. The following secondary outcomes were also explored to identify preliminary evidence of improvements: falls; functional, strength, and balance tests; and patient-reported outcomes. RESULTS: The Aqua Steps intervention exceeded comfortably all feasibility targets set for progression to a large-scale trial; recruitment took 1 month, the program had 88% retention and 90% adherence, and there were no accidents or severe adverse events. After the intervention, falls, fallers, and frequent fallers were reduced by 38%, 36%, and 58%, respectively. There were statistically significant improvements, which were maintained at follow-up, on all functional (22%-70%) and strength (10%-80%) tests, falls efficacy (11%), and balance confidence (8%). In the Steady Steps group, there was a reduction in falls and fallers/frequent fallers (29%-35%) and significant improvements in functional tests (8%-30%) and falls efficacy (7%). CONCLUSIONS: Aqua Steps had very high feasibility and acceptability and was popular and safe. There was preliminary evidence for improvements in falls and risk factors for falls. RELEVANCE: Such positive effects could have a significant impact on people's lives. The findings can inform the design of a large-scale follow-up definitive trial to confirm and generalize findings and to shape future policy on exercise for falls prevention.

articles.title: Reduced Erythropoietic Signalling may be responsible for anemia without iron deficiency among Indian Pregnant Women: findings from a cross-sectional study.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Ravindranadh Palika, Monica Chilumula, Teena Dasi et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: A substantial proportion of anemia is not associated with iron deficiency (ID), particularly in India. However, the aetiology of anemia without ID remains elusive. OBJECTIVE: To compare erythropoietic activity markers (erythropoietin, erythroferrone), micronutrient profiles, and inflammatory markers across four mutually exclusive groups of anemia and iron deficiency (ID) status: anemia with ID, anemia without ID, no-anemia with ID, and no-anemia and no-ID, to identify the factors associated with anemia without ID. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, pregnant women in their third trimester (n=687) were screened for complete blood count including hemoglobin, plasma ferritin (PF), soluble transferrin-receptor (sTfR), high-sensitive C-reactive protein (hsCRP) and Alpha-1-Acid Glycoprotein (AGP), vitamins B12, A, D and red blood cell-folate and in a sub-sample hepcidin, erythropoietin (EPO) and erythroferrone (EFRE) levels were measured. Anemia was defined when Hemoglobin <11g/dL and ID was defined when inflammation adjusted PF levels <20μg/L. RESULTS: The prevalence of anemia with ID, anemia without ID, no-anemia with ID and no-anemia and no ID were 26%, 21%, 11%, 42%, respectively. The anemia with ID group exhibited significantly lower mean Hb (9.32g/dL; 95% CI: 9.1, 9.5 Vs 10.08g/dL 95%CI: 9.9, 10.2), EFRE (0.55ng/mL, 95%CI: 0.5, 0.7 Vs 0.19ng/mL 95%CI: 0.1, 0.3) and higher median EPO (28.18mIU/mL; IQRs: 22.7, 41.0 Vs 22.00mIU/mL; IQRs: 20.8, 24.5) compared to anemia without ID group. Furthermore, despite lower hemoglobin, median EPO in anemia without ID was comparable to non-anemic groups. Micronutrient or Inflammatory markers were either similar or did not show consistent trends across the four groups. Further, hemoglobin levels showed significant negative correlation with EPO (r=-0.55, p<0.001) in anemia with ID group, but not in anemia without ID group (r=0.11, p=0.438). CONCLUSION: Our study findings suggest that reduced erythropoietic signalling may underly anemia without ID, which is not explained by inflammation or micronutrient deficiencies. Thus, diagnosing ID is vital for effective iron treatment.

articles.title: Effects of a multisectoral household agricultural and livelihood intervention on nutrition, development, and morbidity among HIV-affected children 6 to 36 months of age in Western Kenya: A cluster-randomized trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Lisa M Butler, Phelgona Otieno, Bezawit E Kase et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Food insecurity and HIV are interconnected, potentially increasing nutritional and health-related risks. OBJECTIVE: The Pediatric Shamba Maisha study evaluated the effects of an agricultural and livelihood intervention on growth, development, and common morbidities among children in HIV-affected households in Kenya. METHODS: The Pediatric Shamba Maisha study was a parallel-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial nested within a multisectoral agriculture and livelihood intervention trial among food-insecure adults living with HIV in rural Kenya. The Pediatric Study enrolled children aged 6 to 36 months from participating households. Anthropometric and clinical data were collected every 6 months for 24 months. RESULTS: Of the 359 children enrolled (intervention arm=173, control arm=186), 334 (90%) completed the 24-month visit. In 215 children aged 6 to <24 months at enrolment, height/length increased more in the intervention arm than in the control arm (βheight: 1.18 cm, p=0.004, 95% confidence interval (CI) = (0.390,1.98); βheight-for-age z-score: 0.390, p=0.007, 95% CI = (0.109,0.670)). Weight change of children enrolled at aged 6 to <24 months was similar between study arms across 24 months (βweight: -0.126 kg, p=0.299, 95% CI = (-0.3647,0.113); βweight-for-age z-score: -0.099, p=0.279, 95% CI = (-0.278,0.080)). In 142 children aged 24 to 36 months at enrolment, changes in height and weight over time did not differ between arms. For the intervention compared to control, younger children had lower prevalence of cough (β: -0.790 log-odds, p = 0.037, 95% CI = (-1.57,-0.047)), and older children had lower prevalence of diarrhoea (β: -1.66 log-odds, p = 0.017, 95% CI = (-3.03,-0.296)). Neurobehavioral development outcomes did not differ between study arms. CONCLUSIONS: The intervention improved growth and health of children aged 6 to <24 months at enrolment, underscoring the importance of early-life interventions. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifiers: NCT02815579, NCT03170986https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02815579?term=NCT02815579&rank=1https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03170986?term=NCT03170986&rank=1.

articles.title: Assessing dietary intake in infants through fecal sample analysis in the LLNEXT Cohort.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Jurate Gumbaragyte, Caroline Rivera, Anna Bauer et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate diet tracing is fundamental to diet-health association studies, yet it remains challenging. This is particularly the case for early life studies, which rely on parental recall. Fecal sample analysis offers a non-invasive method for assessing those dietary components that have sufficient quantities of DNA remaining in stool, and are able to be taxonomically distinguished by marker gene sequence. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to determine whether a fecal DNA-based approach can be used to characterize infant dietary history. METHODS: We detected food-derived DNA in fecal samples from 73 infants at 9 and 12 months of age (139 samples total) and 25 mothers (25 samples) in the Dutch Lifelines NEXT cohort using FoodSeq, a novel fecal DNA-based tool. We compared FoodSeq data with infant food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) data using logistic mixed-effects models. We also evaluated the coherence of matching FoodSeq/FFQ in relation to the gut microbiome. RESULTS: Infant fecal samples demonstrated a lower diversity in food groups than observed in the mothers. We identified nine significant associations between matching DNA-detected and FFQ-reported food items including nuts (OR = 1.89 [1.24-2.89], q = 0.035), potatoes (OR = 2.16 [1.94-3.91], q = 0.064), dairy (OR = 2.28 [1.20-4.33], q = 0.061), formula feeding (OR = 3.96 [1.58-9.94], q = 0.055), and pork (OR = 2.44 [1.27-4.67], q = 0.063). Matched FFQ/FoodSeq pairs showed significantly stronger associations than unmatched ones (p = 1.6x10-12). Stronger associations of FFQs to gut microbiome taxa showed higher direction concordance with matching FoodSeq items. CONCLUSIONS: Fecal DNA-based diet identification showed evidence for concordance with several caregiver-reported FFQ categories (i.e., potatoes and nuts) in early life, supporting further development and validation of the FoodSeq tool for infant diet assessment up to 12 months of age.

articles.title: Corrigendum to 'Dietary guidelines adherence and pregnancy exposure to 10 classes of priority chemicals: an observational study in the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes Cohort' Am J Clin Nutr. 2026; volume: 124(2) 101393.
articles.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
articles.authors: Diana C Pacyga, Xiaoshuang Xun, Deborah H Bennett et al.

articles.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Marta Mydłowska, Justyna Cichoń-Woźniak, Hanna Dziewiecka et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers. METHODS: Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery. RESULTS: Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences. CONCLUSION: Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

articles.title: A 6-month randomized clinical trial to test the effect of different dietary interventions on abdominal fat components and cardiometabolic profile in overweight adults.
articles.authors: Isa Galvão Rodrigues, Gabriela Maria Pereira Floro Arcoverde, Camila Lima Chagas do Nascimento et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Abdominal obesity is strongly associated with cardiometabolic risk and can be modified through nutritional interventions, yet there is still no consensus on the dietary strategy capable of producing the best outcomes. This study examined the effects of different dietary interventions, with macronutrient management, on abdominal fat components and cardiometabolic parameters in overweight adults. METHODS: A randomized clinical trial was conducted with three individualized dietary interventions involving caloric restriction combined with balanced macronutrient management (BALANCED), carbohydrate reduction (LOWCARB), and fat reduction (LOWFAT), in addition to a control group that received qualitative and group-based counseling (CONTROL). Participants were followed for six months, with assessments at baseline, three, and six months. Visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) were evaluated by ultrasound, along with body weight, biochemical parameters, and blood pressure. RESULTS: Body weight and VAT decreased significantly over time, with no significant time × group interactions, indicating comparable trajectories across the intervention groups. The average weight reduction was ~3%. Significant changes over time were also observed for total cholesterol, glucose, HbA1c, and blood pressure, with no significant time × group interactions for cardiometabolic parameters. CONCLUSION: After six months of dietary intervention, without changes in physical activity level, modest but significant reductions in body weight and VAT were observed over time, with no significant differences in their trajectories among the intervention groups. No evidence of a differential effect of macronutrient composition on these outcomes was observed.
